newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African customs plans blitzes to cut smuggling.
newsitem.headline: S.African customs plans blitzes to cut smuggling.

text.p: South Africa's customs and revenue services will launch random blitzes of border posts and airports to clamp down on rampant smuggling into the country, Commissioner Trevor van Heerden said on Tuesday.
Briefing the parliamentary finance committee on the new South African Revenue Services, the SARS commissioner said one of the strategies included "what we call 10 stings a month."
This would entail targeting certain entry ports and saturating them with officials and police.
"We have to be able to show that we can, in fact, do things and that it can be very effective," he said.
"This will unsettle everybody because they will not know with certainty where we will be going next."

This would be combined with the planned phasing down of the number of legal border posts for commercial imports to 19 from 52 and limiting the number of airports used for imports and exports to eight.

Van Heerden estimated the programme should start swinging into action within the next few months and would be backed up by improved technology and training provided by British and Swedish customs officials.
Other efforts to clamp down on smuggling included tighter control of cargo releases, which used to be based on paperwork, which encouraged fraud.
"We have now just started an electronic cargo release that will reduce fraud," he said.
In addition, minimum values would be set for imports and any goods below those minimum values would be inspected.
The reduction in the March budget of the ad valorem duty to 15 percent from 37.5 percent had already had a major effect on reducing smuggling, especially of electronic goods.
"Legitimate traders are coming to us and saying that they are now back in business," he said.

On the improved collection of revenue, Van Heerden said that, despite the fact that SARS had been going through a transformation process to combine customs and excise and inland revenue, revenue collections had exceeded expectations.
"The indications are at the moment that we have in terms of efficiencies actually exceeded the 1996/97 budget estimate by about 3.1 billion rand," he said.

In the 1996/97 budget, revenue services had been expected to collect an additional 1.5 billion rand. Not only had SARS achieved that target, but it had collected an additional 1.6 billion rand. But both he and SARS chief executive Piet Liebenberg said much remained to be done, despite the successes to date.
